"The recruiters who win are the ones who actually listen when it matters." I wrote that a year ago. But I should be clear what I mean by winning. It's not by closing this candidate. It's about the person you chose to be every time you have a conversation. Hiring is fundamentally a market. One where if you're not hiring the best, someone else is. Where time truly is an asset because if your process takes weeks when another company's is shorter, that might be the difference between your latest rejection or their newest employee. So yes, it's competitive. But competitive doesn't mean we get to forget how to treat people through what's already a brutal process. Here's the part AI hasn't changed: what actually earns a candidate's respect looks the same as it always did. A fair conversation. Paying attention. Listening when the conversation goes sideways — not because it guarantees the hire, but because how you show up when it's not going your way is what people actually remember. That's the win. Even when the offer isn't. What's one conversation with an applicant that went sideways but turned out to matter anyway? ...more

We revamped our office. Every room is named for someone whose resume would have gotten them screened out. Einstein couldn't land an academic job and was filing patents when he rewrote physics. Jensen Huang was washing dishes at Denny's. The Wright brothers were bike mechanics with no engineering training. Goodall was a secretary with no degree. Jack Ma got rejected from 30 jobs, including KFC. Ramanujan was a self-taught clerk in Madras mailing his theorems to Cambridge. Resumes miss people. We built Alex AI because the best person for the job often doesn't look like it on paper. Alex interviews every applicant so nobody gets filtered out before they get a real shot. Now every conference room is a story to tell. ...more

Every time a meeting goes silent, I think about this story my mentor once told me. Two consultants showed up with an empty folder and a claim: the work inside was so refined that only a truly sophisticated hiring manager could actually see it. Anyone who opened it and saw nothing simply wasn't sophisticated enough to see it. Nobody wanted to be the one who saw nothing. The VP of Ops opened the folder first. Called it the most disciplined structure she'd seen all year. The Head of Sales went next. Said it was already better than half his own team's decks. The CFO didn't even open it. Just nodded along and said the ROI spoke for itself. Word got upstairs. Full all-hands announcement. Standing ovation. Everyone congratulating each other on landing this one. Then the newest hire in the building, who hadn't learned the unspoken rule yet, actually opened the folder in front of everyone. It was empty. Completely empty. She said so, out loud. Dead silence. Nobody else in that room had actually looked either. Somebody has to be the one who opens the folder. The lesson? Create a culture that is truth seeking. That's the only way to move in the right direction quickly. ...more

San Francisco is a great city for founders. The talent. The engineers. Other founders. But that's not the whole city. That's just where the tech lives. A few weeks ago I brought the whole team to a Giants game. And there's some sense of awe that strikes you as you look out at the beautiful scenery, from the clouds to the calm waves. This isn't a perfect place. It never has been. There will be nights you're frustrated with it — the rising costs, the commute, feeling like SF is a bubble. And there will be nights you're not. The moment a breakthrough happens in the company. The stranger who helps you carry something up four flights of stairs. The shared ideal of people who chose to build their lives here, same as you did. San Francisco is not just a tech hub. It's a city filled with culture, history, and people worth learning about. Thank you, SF. ...more

Incumbents can't win on the product anymore, so they compete on the rulebook instead. I've watched this happen in industry after industry, and it's happening again right now. Taxi companies couldn't out-compete Uber on price or convenience. So in 2016, Austin's taxi industry got the city to require fingerprint background checks for ride-share drivers, on top of the checks Uber and Lyft already ran. Voters subsequently voted yes on it at the ballot box causing Uber and Lyft to leave the city rather than comply. Hotel chains ran the same play against Airbnb in New York, outspending them on political contributions more than 30 to 1. Local Law 18 passed in 2022, requiring hosts to register and be physically present for any stay under 30 days. It functionally ended most short-term listings in the city. Hotel rates rose within eighteen months. Hotel revenue rose with them, by an estimated $2 billion or more. Neither industry proved the newer competitor was unsafe. They just made it expensive or illegal enough to stop being viable. David Sacks made a similar case this week about a very different industry. He's argued Anthropic and OpenAI are pushing states to adopt tougher AI rules one after another, each stricter law giving the next state cover to go further, weaponizing regulatory uncertainty to lock out open-weight models like China's Kimi K3. Anthropic's own leadership has floated something like an FAA for AI. Sacks' answer: an approval process built for aircraft, on an aircraft's timeline, would be fatal to a technology that ships new versions every few months. Whether or not that's the intent, the mechanism is identical to what taxis and hotels already ran. You don't need to win on the merits if you can make winning on the merits illegal first. Where do you see this playing out before anyone's willing to call it by name? ...more
